forces: Solo violin, two violin parts and viola; continuo silent
performers: John Harrison, violin; Wichita State University Chamber Players; Robert Turizziani, conductor
intro: A goatherd sleeps while leaves rustle and his dog barks beside him. Vivaldi puts all three in the strings: the solo violin dreams, the orchestral violins murmur, and the viola refuses to keep quiet.

sections.label: A · The sleeping goatherd
sections.mNote: Solo violin over rustling violins and the viola’s bark

sections.label: B · The melody reaches G♯ minor
sections.mNote: Long violin notes above a descending-fifths progression

sections.label: A′ · The opening tune returns
sections.mNote: G♯–E–C♯ again, with the same rustling accompaniment

sections.label: C · The violin climbs higher
sections.mNote: The solo reaches a high C♯ before coming down

sections.label: C′ · A repeated C♯-minor cadence
sections.mNote: The solo finishes; the accompanying strings continue

cues.title: Leaves over a sleeping man
cues.text: “E quindi Sul fiorito ameno prato / Al caro mormorio di fronde e piante” — “And then, on the pleasant flowered meadow, to the gentle murmur of leaves and plants.” Vivaldi’s 1725 sonnet places the goatherd under trees. Two violin parts rustle in dotted rhythms; the solo melody begins above them.
cues.evidence: Spring sonnet, letter F; translation ours. Mutopia score after Performers’ Facsimiles, II, bars 1–7: https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=301. The sonnets were published anonymously with Op. 8.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: The dog stays awake
cues.text: “Dorme’l Caprar col fido can’ à lato” — “The goatherd sleeps with his faithful dog beside him.” The viola supplies the bark: two notes, then a rest, marked always very loud and sharply attacked. The continuo is silent throughout. There is nowhere for this dog to hide.
cues.evidence: Spring sonnet, 1725, letter F; translation ours. Mutopia score, II: viola marked Il Cane che grida and sempre molto forte, e Strappato; continuo tacet for all 39 bars: https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=301.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: G♯, E, C♯ again
cues.text: After a cadence in G♯ minor and a bar’s rest, the solo violin returns to its opening three notes: G♯, E, C♯. The leaves have kept rustling through the pause. This time the melody takes a shorter path to C♯ minor.
cues.evidence: Mutopia score, II, bars 18–23; the solo rests in bar 19 and restates its opening in bar 20. José Rodríguez Alvira identifies the third phrase as a variation of the first: https://www.teoria.com/en/articles/2021/vivaldi-seasons/primavera/02.php.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: The girls’ concerts of Venice
cues.text: In 1739 the French traveller Charles de Brosses writes home about Venice’s four girls’ hospitals: concerts of some forty young women, one conducting in a white habit with a bunch of pomegranates at her ear. His favourite is the Pietà, where Vivaldi became violin master in 1703.
cues.evidence: Charles de Brosses, letter XVIII to M. de Blancey, 29 August (1739), Lettres familières écrites d’Italie (ed. Hippolyte Babou, Poulet-Malassis et de Broise, 1858, vol. 1, pp. 141–148): concerts of about forty girls, the young woman in white conducting with pomegranates by her ear, and the Pietà as his favourite and the first for its symphonies; translation ours. https://fr.wikisource.org/wiki/Lettres_famili%C3%A8res_%C3%A9crites_d%E2%80%99Italie_T.1/%C3%80_M._DE_BLANCEY._%E2%80%94_Suite_du_s%C3%A9jour_%C3%A0_Venise Vivaldi became violin master at the Pietà in September 1703: Michael Talbot, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani. https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/antonio-vivaldi_%28Dizionario-Biografico%29/

cues.title: The goatherd sleeps on
cues.text: The violin repeats its last approach to C♯, with a trill on D♯ just before the resolution. It finishes before the other strings. The murmuring violins and the dog’s two-note bark continue for another bar before the accompanying strings hold the final chord.
cues.evidence: Mutopia score, II, bars 34–39: solo cadence in bars 36–37, solo rests in bars 38–39, accompaniment continuing to the final fermata: https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=301.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

transitions.title: The viola walks through fifths
transitions.to: B · The melody reaches G♯ minor
transitions.how: The solo violin repeats its opening G♯–E–C♯, then stretches into longer notes. Underneath, the viola’s barking figure moves through a descending-fifths progression towards G♯ minor. The orchestral violins keep their soft dotted rhythm; the cello remains silent.
transitions.evidence: Mutopia score, II, bars 8–18; the fifths progression and G♯-minor destination are shown by Rodríguez Alvira: https://www.teoria.com/en/articles/2021/vivaldi-seasons/primavera/02.php.

transitions.title: The tune wakes from its rest
transitions.from: B · The melody reaches G♯ minor
transitions.how: The solo holds G♯ at the cadence, then rests for a bar. Its opening G♯–E–C♯ returns over C♯ in the viola. The two accompanying violin parts continue rustling across the pause, so the returning melody arrives inside a sound already in motion.

transitions.title: The violin reaches upwards
transitions.how: The solo starts again with G♯–E–C♯ over C♯ in the viola, then rises to A. The viola moves to F♯ and D♯ beneath the longer phrase. The violin climbs as high as C♯ before descending towards its final cadence.
transitions.evidence: Mutopia score, II, bars 24–33, solo violin and viola; harmonic progression discussed at https://www.teoria.com/en/articles/2021/vivaldi-seasons/primavera/02.php.

transitions.title: The cadence comes round again
transitions.how: The solo repeats C♯–F♯–A from the preceding phrase. Its D♯ trill resolves to C♯ over the viola’s G♯–C♯ cadence. The violin then rests while the accompanying parts finish their rustling and barking on a held C♯-minor chord.

composer.epithet: He wrote concertos for the women of Venice’s Pietà, operas for its theatres, and a barking dog for the viola.
facts: Violin with his father Giovanni Battista, a player at St Mark’s, Venice
Pietà violin teacher from 1703; maestro de’ concerti from 1716; court service in Mantua, 1718–20
More than 500 concertos, operas, sacred music and sonatas
composer.background:
In 1703 a twenty-five-year-old Venetian became a priest in March and a violin teacher in September. Antonio Vivaldi had red hair, a formidable bow arm and a chest complaint that made celebrating Mass difficult. His father Giovanni Battista had been a barber before joining the violinists at St Mark’s; he taught Antonio and continued helping with his career long after the son had become famous. Venice knew Antonio as il prete rosso, the red priest. His working places would be the chapel, the orchestra gallery and the opera house.

The Ospedale della Pietà cared for abandoned children. Its musical establishment was a selected group of girls and women, trained to sing and play to a standard that brought visitors from across Europe. Some remained there as adult musicians and teachers. Vivaldi taught the advanced string players, rehearsed the orchestra and supplied new pieces. The governors voted on his employment each year: in 1709 they dispensed with him, and in 1711 took him back. The music survived the office politics.
